Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger for a life-threatening illness trauma unless there was a very specific exposure context; the other items point more toward nightmares/body sensations/illness-related reexperiencing, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other threat and memory items describe fear, bodily alarm, pain, sensory recall, and dysregulated emotion rather than impulsive or reckless responding, so this item stands out as clinically disconnected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette: Karim al-Mansour, a 38-year-old American of Lebanese descent living alone, had spent the better part of the last year retreating from a world that suddenly felt fundamentally unsafe. Six months prior, a severe autoimmune crisis had plunged him into a critical care unit where every breath felt borrowed. The hospitalization was defined by the relentless intrusion of medical procedures: nurses adjusting his central line, the sharp pinch of diagnostic taps against his abdomen, and the constant, invasive monitoring that stripped him of autonomy. Photographs from that time captured his hollowed face next to coiled tubes and sterile drapes, images that now sat on his phone’s locked screen, untouched and heavy. When the trauma subsided and he returned to his daily life, the salon he had run for a decade became a landscape of landmines. It was during his second week back, wiping down his station after a client left, that the first fracture appeared. A routine tube of antiseptic hand gel caught his eye, and the visual of its white cap instantly triggered a violent physical reactivity. His breath hitched, his heart hammered against his ribs, and a wave of horror and shame flooded his chest. His body was on alert, coiled tight and ready to flee, as if the danger were still in the room. This sudden physiological storm did not stop at his skin. It pulled him directly into the memory of the ward. Just as quickly, an olfactory recall washed over him—the sharp, chemical tang of the salon’s floor cleaner morphing in his mind into the sterile, copper scent of the hospital corridors. The association was immediate and inescapable. As the memory took hold, pain recall struck; the exact pressure he felt during the intubation brace throbbed in his sternum, stripping away any context and leaving only emotion without image, a raw, nameless dread that his body was failing him. The initial flood of sensations quickly hardened into a rigid set of beliefs. Karim had come to view his own physiology as an enemy, a traitor that kept reacting as if he were still in the ICU even when he was safe on his couch. This conviction that his body was utterly unreliable bred a quiet, gnawing fear that he was going crazy. The appraisal that his mind was fracturing did not remain passive. It fed his threat system, amplifying his negative emotions until his baseline state was one of constant bodily tension. He walked through his days with his shoulders braced, his jaw clenched, convinced that any sudden spike in anxiety was proof of his unraveling. This internal distrust did not merely sit in his head; it actively shaped what he noticed. His belief that he could no longer trust his internal signals made him hyper-vigilant to environmental cues, instantly dialing his threat response to a fever pitch. When a friend texted to say, “I heard you’re seeing a doctor again,” the phrase acted as a trigger, instantly reinforcing his appraisal that his body was a broken system. His body surged with physical reactivity, his palms sweating and his vision tunneling, mirroring the exact physiological cascade he experiences during procedures. The cycle tightened over the following months, calcifying into a pattern that severed him from his work and his community. Avoidance became a reflex. He stopped answering shift requests, telling the salon owner he was taking a sabbatical, though he knew it was a retreat from the fear of losing control. He avoided grocery stores, canceled his dentist appointment, and kept a bottle of water on his nightstand to ground himself when he woke from a nightmare, the dream residue leaving him gasping and convinced the crisis was returning. Yet, the more he tried to suppress his reactions, the more power the memories held. The memory of his hospitalization became a magnet for his fear. When the memory returned, the emotional intensity stripped away context, flooding his system with immediate threat. It didn’t just cause physical reactivity; it pulled him directly toward medical triggers. He found himself searching hospital forums, his phone screen lit by the blue glow of patient diagrams, unable to look away. This compulsive checking only fed his threat perception. The sustained mental focus on his symptoms kept his nervous system in a permanent state of alarm, which in turn pulled him deeper into the memory of his illness. Each spike of negative emotions and bodily tension validated his core belief, creating a seamless loop where fear and memory constantly reinforced the sensation of threat. Now, Karim sits in the quiet waiting room of a community clinic, his hands knotted in his lap. The hair clips and shears that once defined his identity gather dust on a shelf at home, a concrete monument to a life put on hold. What finally brought him through the door was a panic attack in his shower, where the spray pattern perfectly mimicked the mist of his nebulizer treatments, pushing him to acknowledge that isolation was not protecting him. He is terrified that the therapist will see him as fundamentally broken, that the machinery beneath his skin is permanently fractured. What he hopes for, with a fragile certainty, is simply to stop bracing for a collapse that no longer exists, to believe that his pulse is a rhythm and not a warning, and to return to his chair without feeling like he is standing on an operating table.
